thread.title: Most of the dire predictions about the stock market don’t make sense — but some do - MarketWatch

author: Tim Mullaney
title: Most of the dire predictions about the stock market don’t make sense — but some do - MarketWatch
text:
TriStar Pictures / Courtesy: Everett Collection What’s hiding in your portfolio? Whenever stocks go through a plunge like December’s 7.2% drop in the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA, -1.49% — that’s 7.8% on the Standard & Poor’s 500 SPX, -1.54% , setting up its first year-long total-return decline since 2008 — there are always lots of explanations.
And many panicked explanations of how things can get worse, soon.
Fortunately, most of those explanations and predictions don’t make sense. A few usually make some — which is different than saying they’re true.
But it’s useful to screen these stories, if only to focus on what’s really important. Let’s screen out some obvious non-issues first, then move on to things small investors like you should worry about. All in 850 words.
Okay? Let’s go. Spoiler alert: This is mostly about fear — rational and irrational — of the Federal Reserve.
Read our up-to-the-minute coverage of the Federal Reserve’s announcement.
We’re all so indebted the sky will surely fall Ah, no.
Everyone would like less debt, but America’s debt burdens aren’t high. Thanks partly to still-low interest rates, household debt payments as a percent of income are 30% lower (10% v 13%, per the Fed) than in 2006 and lower than anytime since at least 1985. That’s true even with the student-loan explosion.
Corporations are so indebted, surely the sky will fall They’re really not — and even corporations’ debt is cheap.
Yes, corporate debt is up — but so are earnings before interest, taxes and non-cash depreciation and amortization charges. According to Moody’s Investor Service, corporate-debt payments only take about 10% of EBITDA. It’s as if you made $100,000 a year, lived on $80,000 (leaving $20,000 after cash expenses) and paid $2,000 in debt service. It wouldn’t break you.
This is one reason Moody’s says corporate debt defaults are low and headed lower — only 66 corporations defaulted on public debt worldwide in the 12 months ending in November, down from 91 a year earlier. These aren’t numbers of which economic busts are made.
The yield curve inverted, so surely the sky will fall Closer, but still no. A new paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis explains that when short-term interest rates move higher than longer-term rates, it does imply slowing growth in consumer spending — but still no recession. Instead, it means the economy is more vulnerable to a shock, like 2008’s mortgage-bond meltdown. But absent a shock we can’t see, no recession.
Stock valuations are insane, so surely the sky will fall More than half of Russell 2000 RUT, -2.20% stocks are 20% cheaper than their peaks, so we’re already in a bear market by that standard. The “most overvalued” stocks in the mind of popular critics are usually technology issues — but as of this morning Apple AAPL, -3.12% was down 29%, Facebook FB, -7.25% 34%, Microsoft MSFT, -0.27% 11%, Netflix NFLX, -1.62% 36% Amazon AMZN, -3.64% 24% and Google parent Alphabet GOOG, -0.56% 19% from 52-week highs.
S&P 500 companies are trading at an aggregate 14.7 times expected 2019 earnings, according to S&P Capital IQ. That’s relatively low.
Now let’s talk about some things that might actually be worrisome.
China could matter It’s not as overloaded with debt as some think, and is still immature enough as an economic power that its growth is more secular than cyclical. But it does have cycles in its own fashion — its last slowdown punished Apple in 2015-16 — and U.S. trade policy could slow Chinese demand for U.S. goods, hurting American corporate profits. Trade wars, it turns out, aren’t easy to win.
Corporate profits matter — a lot — and they are poised to weaken S&P Capital IQ says 2019 profits will rise 5% from 2018 — down from 10% estimated in September. That means actual declines for many companies, and reaction won’t be pretty. Some declines may be about trade, and others may be driven by interest rates or collapsing oil prices. So regular investors should watch earnings closely and skeptically.
But, CFRA Research stock strategist Sam Stovall points out that broad corporate earnings declines — he calls them “earnings recessions” — have only led to real recessions about half of the time since 1950. Plus, stocks’ 13% drop since July is already more than the 10% drop he said usually accompanies earnings dips.
Then there are interest rates The consensus view has been that the Fed would raise interest rates today and three times in 2019. But the recent housing slowdown, and stubbornly sluggish corporate investment, suggest rates are already rising too fast. And this year’s fiscal stimulus is set to wane, making tight money likely to bite into growth harder. Finally, that cozy picture of easy-to-manage debt service gets less so as rates rise, trimming consumer purchasing power.
So what should the Fed do?
The Fed’s role since 2010 has been Washington’s adult, providing monetary stimulus when Congress wouldn’t prime the pump, and, more recently, leaning into President Donald Trump’s late-in-the-cycle stimulus by tightening money.
But the president’s role is different now. With his trade bluster, and bluster generally. he’s a drag on market confidence and the real economy. Since he wants the Fed to slow its tightening, many would see a pause as central bankers irresponsibly siding with the president.
But a pause would simply mean the Fed is continuing its role of supplying the defects of elected branches, to lift a phrase from the Federalist Papers. The difference is that those defects are so severe now, and so very obvious.
